summary: At nearly 39 square miles but only about 23,000 residents, Ramona sprawls across an inland valley northeast of San Diego with a population density closer to a ranching town than a suburb — and that's exactly what it was for most of its history. The Santa Maria Valley floor sits around 1,400 feet in elevation, ringed by boulder-studded hills and chaparral ridgelines that catch golden light in a way the coast never does, with annual daytime highs averaging a dry 74°F and nearly ten hours of sunshine per day. The tradeoff for that open-sky setting is isolation: there's no freeway through town, and commutes into central San Diego run 45 minutes to over an hour on winding SR-67, making this firmly a bedroom community where most wage earners drive out for work in healthcare, defense, or service-sector jobs clustered closer to the coast. A median home price around $704,500 against a median household income just above $101,000 yields a price-to-income ratio near seven — steep, though monthly rents hovering near $1,800 offer a less punishing entry point. Main Street carries a handful of restaurants, a weekly farmers' market, and western-heritage retail that gives the town a distinct rural-commercial identity rather than a copy-paste suburban one. Ramona is essentially a wide, quiet valley where space and sky come at the cost of connectivity to everything else in the county.
